title: "Sound 5: LFOs"
toc: true

An **LFO**, or **low-frequency oscillator**, is an oscillator too slow to hear as a pitch,
typically between a tenth of a beat and twenty times a second. Instead of being listened to, it
*moves a control*: the pitch, the volume, a filter, the stereo position. Almost every effect that
"moves" (vibrato, tremolo, wah, chorus, phaser, PWM) is an LFO turning a knob for you.

**How to use the page.** Press ▶ or play the keys. The strip above the scope draws the LFO itself
over the last two seconds; the red dot is where it is now.

## What an LFO can move

<div class="sk" data-w="lfo"></div>

Leave the shape on **Sine** and try each target with **Rate** about 5 Hz:

- **Pitch** gives **vibrato**: the note bends slightly sharp and flat. Singers and string players
  use 5 to 7 cycles a second. Too deep and it sounds seasick; too fast and it sounds nervous.
- **Volume** gives **tremolo**: the note gets louder and softer. The "tremolo" on a guitar amp is
  this, and so is a vibraphone with its motor on.
- **Filter cutoff** gives an automatic **wah**. Slow it right down (0.2 Hz) for a slowly opening and
  closing sound; speed it up for a "wobble" bass.
- **Pan** moves the sound between your left and right ear (**auto-pan**). Use headphones.

**Depth** is how far the LFO moves the control, and **Rate** is how fast. Those two plus the shape
are all an LFO has.

## Shapes

- **Sine** and **triangle**: smooth back-and-forth.
- **Square**: jumps between two values. On pitch it's a trill; on volume, a chopped "gate".
- **Sawtooth (ramp)**: rises slowly, then drops. On pitch it sounds like a siren.
- **Random (sample & hold)**: jumps to a new random value every cycle. On the filter it's the
  bubbling "computer" sound of 1970s science fiction.

## When an LFO gets fast enough to hear

Set the target to **Volume**, the shape to **Sine** and slowly push the rate past 20 Hz. The
tremolo stops sounding like a pulse and becomes a rough, buzzy tone, and new pitches appear on the
spectrum on both sides of the note. That is **amplitude modulation**. Do the same with **Pitch** and
past about 30 Hz the vibrato becomes a metallic, bell-like timbre: that is **frequency modulation**,
the subject of [Sound 7](sound-fm.qmd). An LFO and an audible oscillator are the same thing at
different speeds.

## LFOs elsewhere on these pages

- The **PWM** in [Sound 2](sound-waveforms.qmd) is an LFO on the pulse width.
- **Chorus** ([Sound 12](sound-chorus.qmd)) is an LFO on a very short delay.
- A **phaser** ([Sound 13](sound-phaser.qmd)) is an LFO sweeping a chain of filters.
- The **Leslie** speaker in the [organ lesson](arrange-organ.qmd) is a mechanical LFO: a spinning
  horn moves pitch, volume and direction all at once.
